title: What Freud Really Thought About Women
the_thought: He thought a woman was a man who had lost something.
hook: The chair is empty. The hour is not over. A young woman has put on her coat and walked out of Berggasse 19. Sigmund Freud keeps the folder. He writes her down anyway. People later said he explained women. But he did not. So what did he think about women? He thought a woman was a man who had lost something. That is the thought. The rest is a case that quit, a map he drew anyway, a colleague who said the map was backwards, a daughter who stayed, and a riddle he never answered. The folder stays. Cream board. Red ribbon. Thick enough to slap the desk. He will print it. She will not come back. If you want his thought, do not start with a statue. Start with an empty chair and a file that outlived the person who left. The file is cream. The ribbon is red. The chair is still warm from a person who decided the hour was over. That is the whole opening picture. An empty hour. A kept file. A thought that starts with the boy and never quite finishes the girl. Keep the folder in your hand. We will come back to it.

levels.name: Walkout
beats: She is eighteen. Her real name is Ida Bauer. Freud will publish her as Dora. He does not ask if she wants that name. Her father, a textile man, brings her to the couch in October 1900. She has a cough. She has lost her voice. She has written a suicide note her parents found. The grown ups want the doctor to fix the girl so the house can stay quiet. The house is not quiet. Years earlier the family stayed near a married couple. The wife nursed the father. The husband took the girl on walks and brought gifts. When she was about fourteen, that husband tried to kiss her. She said no. She told her parents. The grown ups treated the no like a scene that threatened the father's friendship. Freud treats the no like a clue. For about eleven weeks she comes to Berggasse 19. He decides the cough is a story about desire. He decides she is in love with the man she refused. He decides her silence is a yes she cannot admit. She tells him that sounds ridiculous. On the last day of 1900 she stands up. She does not book another hour. Freud is stung. He writes that she has acted out a revenge. He sits with the folder. Cream board. Red ribbon. Fat as a brick. In April 1902 she comes back once. She says she confronted the couple, and that they confessed she had been right. She has a pain in her face. He still reads the body as a message. Then she is gone again. He writes the case in 1901 and waits. He prints it in 1905 as Fragment of an Analysis of a Case of Hysteria. Fragment. He named the unfinished thing in the title. Years later he adds a footnote and blames himself for missing another attachment in the story. He does not unpublish the file. The folder gets a public life. The girl does not come back to edit it. He thought he had seen inside a woman. What he had was a teenager who left. Her brother Otto will become a famous politician. That is not this story. This story is the file. Ida Bauer later marries. She has a son. In 1939 she leaves Europe and dies in New York in 1945. We do not invent her private thoughts. We have his printed case, her exit, one short return, and the name he chose for her. Later readers will fight over whether he helped her or used her. Hold the folder. Same cream board. Same red ribbon. He will keep writing woman into files like this. The first big file walked out. That walkout is not a side story. It is the picture this title owns. A doctor who is sure. A chair that goes cold. A folder that stays warm. If you want his thought about women, start here. Not with a slogan. With a girl who said no, a man who heard yes, and a file that outlived them both. The walkout is the first no. The theory will be the second. He does not change the map because the chair went empty. He prints the map. That is the habit this title has to show. Sure man. Cold chair. Warm folder. The hour ended. The sentence did not. He also writes that he failed as an analyst because he missed the heat in the room, the way she used him. That is his later note, not her diary. We keep it as his note. We do not turn it into her confession. The Interpretation of Dreams is already out when he drafts the file in 1901. This case is the next public test. He lets it sit four years. Later teachers will assign the fragment as if it were a window. It is a folder. A named girl. A quit hour. A doctor who kept the last word. Watch for the next move. He will turn one quit case into a rule for every girl. That is the whole engine. The lake, the gifts, the no, the parents who wanted peace, the eleven weeks, the last day of 1900, the 1902 return, the 1905 print. Those are the facts. The thought is what he does with them. He does not let the walkout close the folder. He opens it for strangers. Cream board. Red ribbon. A public life for a private hour. That is the first picture this title owns, and it is enough to start a twenty minute story if we stay with what he did next.

levels.name: Little Men
beats: The theory comes later, in public papers, not only in that folder. In 1905, the same year the Dora file goes public, he publishes Three Essays on the Theory of Sexuality. He writes as if the boy is the clear case and the girl is the harder copy. The boy is the template. The girl is the problem copy. In 1908, in On the Sexual Theories of Children, he is already talking about a girl who looks at a boy and decides she has been shorted. He is not telling a joke in a salon. He is building a ladder. First a child. Then a look. Then a verdict. In 1912, in an essay on love, he borrows an old line from Napoleon. Anatomy is destiny. He lets it sit near desire as if the body had already written the ending. In 1923 he writes on the infantile genital organization. In 1924 he writes on the end of the Oedipus complex. The little girl, he says, starts on the same road as the little boy. Then she sees a difference. Then she feels she has lost something. The boy keeps his first love and his first body story. The girl, in this telling, must switch both. In 1925 he makes it a system. The paper is called Some Psychical Consequences of the Anatomical Distinction Between the Sexes. He says a small girl sees the difference, feels she has been castrated, and falls a victim to envy for the penis. That envy, he says, can turn into a wish for a child, or a grudge against the mother, or a lifelong feeling of being less. He is not whispering. He is printing a map. Start with the boy. Then explain the girl as the boy minus something. He thought a woman was a man who had lost something. Say it again. That is not a slogan later critics invented to trap him. It is the shape of his own pages. A girl, in this story, has extra work. She must change what counts as her body. She must change who she first loves. A boy, he says, gets to keep both. Two extra jobs for the girl. Zero extra jobs for the boy. Keep the picture simple enough for a child. He thought girls started as little men, then found out they were not, and spent a life wanting the missing piece. That is a hard sentence. It is also his. If you want a kind Freud on this title, you will not find him in those papers. You will find a man who thinks female development is a longer, later, incomplete version of male development. He will add folds. He will not throw the map away. The folder on the desk was one girl. The papers are all girls. He moves from a quit case to a rule. That is how a thought becomes a system. The walkout could have taught him to doubt the reading. Instead it becomes a specimen. The cream folder stays in the room while the map grows teeth. People who only know the later riddle skip these pages. Do not skip them. The riddle is late. The map is early. The map is the thought. A child can draw it. Two paper dolls. One with a pocket. One without. He called the missing pocket destiny. Readers who meet him only through jokes about cigars will miss this. This is not a joke. This is a printed ladder from 1905 to 1925. Each rung makes the girl more like a delayed boy. The last rung gives the delay a name. Envy. Inferiority. A wish that is really a substitute. That is the system. The folder was the rehearsal. One essay on what he calls aberrations. One on children. One on later life. The girl is not the hero of any of them. 1923 and 1924 are the tightening years, not a change of heart. The infantile genital story and the end of the Oedipus story both keep the boy as the easy road. The girl is the delay. The delay becomes envy. The envy becomes a wish, a grudge, a feeling of being less. That chain is the 1925 paper. Readers who meet him only through jokes about cigars will miss this. This is not a joke. This is a printed ladder from 1905 to 1925. Each rung makes the girl more like a delayed boy. The last rung gives the delay a name. That is the system. The folder was the rehearsal. When he says anatomy is destiny in 1912, he is not writing a slogan for a later poster. He is borrowing Napoleon to bless a body story he already believes. Keep the ladder in your head. Child. Look. Verdict. Extra jobs. Substitute wish. That is female development as he printed it. Not a mystery. A sequence. The later hole does not erase the sequence.

levels.name: Horney's No
beats: Then the people in the room stop nodding. Karen Horney is an analyst, a woman, and she has read the map. In 1926 she publishes The Flight from Womanhood. She writes that psychoanalysis is the creation of a male genius, and that it is no surprise the theory understands men more easily than women. She does not call him a fool. She says the starting picture is wrong. Maybe boys envy what women can do. Pregnancy. Birth. A body that can make a person. Maybe that is the envy the first map hid. Maybe culture, not a missing part, is what makes a girl feel small. She turns the ladder around. If the first picture is a boy, of course the girl looks like a loss. Change the first picture and the loss may be a story men told. Helene Deutsch stays closer to Freud. She will later write a whole psychology of women that still walks his road. Other women in the circle split. Some will later write that womanliness is a mask a person puts on. We should not turn every later paper into this title. This title needs the no he heard while he was still alive. Freud reads them. In the 1933 lecture on femininity he mentions that some analysts want to shrink that first penis-envy and treat it as secondary, later, smaller. He says he still bets on the early infantile factor. He hears the no. He keeps the map. That is the contradiction this title needs. The folder on the desk was already a girl who said no. Now a colleague says no to the theory. He publishes anyway. He is not a man who never met women who thought. He is a man who met them and still started the story with the boy. Horney keeps working. In the early 1930s she leaves for the United States. The no leaves the room. The map stays on the Viennese desk. The argument does not end in 1926. It becomes the fight later readers inherit. We should not turn her paper into a victory parade. We should not pretend he recanted. He answered by repeating the early factor, only louder. The map gets a footnote. The map stays. A child can retell this beat. A woman in the room said the picture starts in the wrong place. The man who drew it said the first picture was still right. Two desks. A gap of floor between them. No handshake that rewrites the page. If you came for a conversion scene, you will not get one. You will get a published no, and a published anyway. That is more honest than a film where he suddenly understands. He did not. The folder already taught us that habit. Horney is not a later blog. She is in the room in 1926, writing in the same professional language, saying the first doll is wrong. That is why her no belongs on a chapter card. Not because she wins. Because he hears her and does not move the first doll. She is not denying that girls suffer. She is denying that the first cause is a missing part. Culture can teach a girl she is less. A theory written mostly by men can mistake that lesson for anatomy. That is The Flight from Womanhood in one blunt cartoon. Helene Deutsch will later write a psychology of women that still walks his road. That split matters. The circle is not a choir. It is a room with two maps on the table and only one of them on the lecture stand in 1933. When he mentions dissenters, he names the disagreement so he can keep the early factor. That is not a conversion. That is a controlled footnote. Horney leaving for the United States in the early 1930s is not the victory scene. It is the no walking out of the building, the way the first girl walked out of the hour. Two walkouts. One patient. One colleague. He prints through both. The first doll stays.

levels.name: Dark Continent
beats: In 1926, in The Question of Lay Analysis, he writes the line later posters love. We know less about little girls than about boys. The sexual life of adult women, he says, is a dark continent for psychology. He puts the words in marks, like a traveler's phrase. He is not saying he has finished the map. He is saying the map has a hole. Hold that hole. A cream map with a dark oval cut out. Lamp light through the gap. No country names. In 1931 he writes Female Sexuality and admits the first attachment to the mother lasts longer in girls than he used to think. His own earlier story was too simple. The girl, he now says, stays with the first love longer than the boy does. That is a real revision. It is also not a new first picture. He adds a fold. He does not throw the map away. Then in 1933 he gives Lecture 33, Femininity, in the New Introductory Lectures on Psycho-Analysis. He opens with the old riddle of the nature of femininity. He tells the men in the room they have knocked their heads against it. He tells the women the lecture will not apply to them. You are yourselves the problem. That line is in the printed lecture. It is not a joke we added. He says psychoanalysis does not try to describe what a woman is. It tries to say how she comes into being from a child with a bisexual disposition. Two extra jobs, he says. Change the zone that matters. Change the first love. A boy, again, gets to keep both. That is the little-man map said in a hall. And still he leaves the dark hole on the page. He can write a whole lecture on how a girl becomes a woman and still call adult women a continent he has not mapped. Both things are him. The shrug and the system. At the end of the lecture he says the picture is incomplete and does not always sound friendly. He says he has been describing women only as far as one function goes, and that a woman may be a human being in other respects as well. Then he tells the room, if they want more, ask their own life, or ask the poets, or wait for science. That last shrug is not kindness. It is him handing the unfinished sentence to someone else after he has already printed the map. A child can hold both pictures. He drew a girl as a boy who lost something. He also drew a hole and called it a continent. People who want only the monster skip the hole. People who want only the riddle skip the map. This title needs both. The folder was sure. The lecture is sure and lost at the same time. That is why the empty chair still matters. He could fill a hall and still leave a hole in the paper. Remember the year. 1926 is also Horney's year. The same season he names the continent he has not mapped, she names the map as a male invention. He prints the hole. She prints the protest. He does not choose between them. He keeps both on the shelf and lectures from the old first picture. That is not confusion. That is a choice. The 1931 fold about the long mother-tie is the closest he comes to saying his first girl-story was too thin. He says it, then he still tells the hall in 1933 that a girl has two extra jobs. The hole and the jobs sit in the same decade. A child can hold both. A cream map with a dark oval. A chalkboard with two extra marks next to the girl and none next to the boy. That is the lecture. Incomplete, he says. Not always friendly, he says. Then he points at poets and future science. He has already used the present tense of science for the little-man map. The pointing is late.

levels.name: Anna Stays
beats: There is one woman who does not walk out. Anna is the youngest daughter. She becomes an analyst of children. She stays in the work when others leave the room. She sits at a second desk while the first desk still owns the map. In 1938 the family has to leave Vienna. Marie Bonaparte helps them go. No flags in this picture. A closed trunk on a night platform. Steam. One suitcase. A second life in London. Anna keeps the desk. She writes about children. She becomes the heir of a method, not the answer to a title. Do not turn her into a secret kind Freud on women. A daughter who stays is not a theory that changed. It is a life that did not quit. The walkout was a patient. The stay is a child of the house. Those are not the same no, and they are not the same yes. If you use Anna to wash the 1925 paper, you are doing what the posters do. We will not do that. We will put her in the last rooms because she is in the last rooms. Berggasse 19 goes quiet. The couch will later sit behind a rope. The folder does not need a new city. The thought already traveled in print. Anna carrying the method to London is a fact. Anna rewriting the little-man map is not a fact we have. So the picture is simple. One girl left the hour. One woman kept the work. Neither event tells us he thought women were finished people on their own terms. He thought a woman was a man who had lost something. A loyal daughter does not cancel a printed map. A night train does not cancel a lecture. Keep them in the story so the story does not pretend he lived in a room with no women. He lived with women. Patients. Colleagues. A daughter. A princess who later booked the tickets. He still started the girl as a copy of the boy. That is the thought, even in the last rooms. London rain on a grey window. Stacked child notebooks. No new first picture on the cover. In 1936 she publishes The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence. It is a book about how a mind protects itself. It is not a recantation of Lecture 33. After the family leaves, the children's work continues. Students will learn her name as a founder of child analysis. That is a real career. It still does not rewrite 1925. Keep the two facts on the table and do not stir them into one sweet ending. She is not a patient in this chapter. She is the heir of a method. The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence, 1936, is a book about how a mind protects itself. Students will learn her name as a founder of child analysis. That is a real career. It still does not rewrite 1925. Keep the two facts on the table and do not stir them into one sweet ending. Bonaparte booking the 1938 tickets is another fact. No flags. A trunk. Steam. London rain. The museum rope comes later. The method crosses a border. The first picture does not. That is why this chapter exists in a twenty minute cut. Without it, the story looks like he lived in a room with no women except the one who quit. He lived with women. He still started the girl as a copy of the boy. The stay is not the recantation. The stay is the household continuing.

levels.name: Unanswered
beats: Late in the story a princess sits in the chair. Marie Bonaparte comes to analysis in 1925. She is a patient and later a colleague. She will help get him out of Vienna in 1938. Ernest Jones, Freud's biographer, later writes that Freud said to her the great question he still could not answer, after thirty years on the feminine soul, was what a woman wants. Was will das Weib. We do not have Freud's own letter with that line. We have Jones telling us Bonaparte told him. A concordance of his collected works does not find those English words as his. A 2025 paper in History of Psychology goes back to her notebooks and treats the line as disputed in context. Treat it as a reported line, not a carved tablet. Even if the words are right, they do not cancel the papers. The papers already said what he thought. He thought a woman was a man who had lost something. The riddle is him admitting the map never closed. People love the riddle because it sounds humble. The papers are not humble. The papers are a system. A system can have a hole and still be a system. That is the last reversal. The unanswered question is not proof he had no thought. It is proof he would not let the thought finish. The rooms at Berggasse 19 are a museum now. The couch sits behind a rope. Visitors take photographs of an empty chair. The theory is still argued in 2026. No new letter has arrived that washes the map. We should not pretend he had no map. He had one. It started with the boy. It ended with a shrug he printed as science. People who wanted a secret kind Freud on women will not get him from the files. People who wanted only a monster will miss the hole he named. The honest sentence is smaller than both posters. He thought a girl was a boy who had lost something, and he never trusted that he had finished the sentence. The chair is still in the museum photograph. The folder is still the object. Cream board. Red ribbon. Fat as a brick. The map is still the thought. That is what Freud really thought about women. Not a riddle on a poster. A walkout, a little-man map, a colleague's no, a dark hole, a daughter who stayed, and a question he let other people repeat. The folder stays. The girl does not. If a later age wants a kinder first picture, it will have to draw it. He already drew his. Bonaparte is not a punch line. She sat in the chair. She later sat at the table of the work. Jones put her sentence in a biography and the sentence left the book. Posters are easier than the 1925 paper. This video is the paper, the walkout, and the hole. The poster can wait. The folder cannot. Cream board. Red ribbon. Still shut. Bonaparte is not a punch line. She sat in the chair. She later sat at the table of the work. Jones put her sentence in a biography, 1953, and the sentence left the book. A 2014 check of the concordance finds hundreds of women and not that English question as his line. The 2025 notebook paper makes the context even less like a carved tablet. This video is the paper, the walkout, and the hole. The poster can wait. The folder cannot. Cream board. Red ribbon. Still shut. Visitors in 2026 still photograph the empty chair. That is fine. Photograph the chair. Then read 1925. Then read Horney 1926. Then read Lecture 33. Then decide if the riddle was humility or a hole he named after he had already drawn the girl as a delayed boy. This title's answer is the drawing, not the poster. He already drew his. A later age that wants a kinder first picture will have to draw it on a new page.
What he thought about the mind itself is another story. That one is next.
